title: Case study: What is Union Pacific worth?

questions.prompt: Figures in this quiz come from Union Pacific's annual reports (Form 10-K) and the case. In 2025 the railroad had operating income of $9,846 million, depreciation of $2,465 million, capital investments of $3,791 million and a $361 million investment in working capital. With a 24.1% tax rate, what was its free cash flow? Answer in millions of dollars to the nearest million.

Free cash flow in 2030, the last forecast year, is $7,194 million. It grows 3% a year after that, and the WACC is 7.57%. What is the terminal value at the end of 2030? Answer in billions of dollars to one decimal.
questions.explanation: TV = FCF_2030 × 1.03 / (0.0757 − 0.03) = 7,409.8 / 0.0457 = 162,140 million, about $162.1 billion. Discounted five years at 7.57% it is worth about $112.6 billion today.

questions.prompt: The enterprise value is $139,872 million, net debt is $24,984 million and there are 593.4 million shares. What is the value per share? Answer in dollars to two decimals.
The case discounts free cash flow at the WACC and then subtracts net debt. Why?
choices: Because the cost of equity is always lower than the WACC
Because debt is paid out of revenue before operating income is measured
Because free cash flow belongs to lenders and shareholders together, so its value is the whole firm, and shareholders get what is left after the debt
Because the 10-K reports free cash flow after interest has been paid
questions.explanation: Free cash flow is the cash available to everyone who financed the firm. Discounting it at the WACC values the whole enterprise; subtracting what is owed to lenders, net of cash, leaves the shareholders' part.

questions.prompt: The share price implies long-run growth of 3.79% a year. Union Pacific reinvests 16.6% of its after-tax operating income. Using growth = reinvestment share × return on new investment, what return must new investment earn? Answer as a percent to one decimal.
questions.explanation: Return on new investment = 3.79 / 16.6 = 0.228, or 22.8%. The report puts the railroad's return on invested capital at 16.3% in 2025, so the price needs new projects to earn much more than the existing railroad, or more reinvestment.

questions.prompt: The base case values a share at $193.61 and the market price was $235.10. Which statement does the case support?
choices: The stock was overpriced, so it should have been sold
With every other input at the base case, the price implies long-run growth of about 3.8% a year
The share price will fall to $193.61 within five years
The gap must come from an error in the annual report
questions.explanation: Turning the model around shows what the price assumes: 3.79% long-run growth, or a 47% margin, or a 6.89% WACC. That is a statement about assumptions, not a prediction or a recommendation.

questions.prompt: In 2,000 random draws, 3.5% value the share at or above the market price. What does that number mean?
choices: Under the ranges this case chose, 3.5% of the draws give a value at or above the price
There is a 3.5% chance that the share price will rise
Union Pacific will be worth $235.10 or more 3.5% of the time
3.5% of analysts agree with the market price
questions.explanation: The draws describe the ranges the case chose. Widening one end of one range, long-run growth to 5%, raises the share to 22.6%. The number is a property of the assumptions, not a probability about the stock.

questions.prompt: Which input's uncertainty widens the spread of values the most in this case?
questions.explanation: Fixing long-run growth at 3% narrows the middle 80% of values from $55.86 wide to $33.13 wide. Fixing either of the others narrows it by less than $5. Long-run growth drives the terminal value, which is 80% of the firm's value.
